stories.headline: Columbus Crew 2 fires Higuain after fallout from ref abuse
stories.summary: The Columbus Crew announced that Crew 2 manager Federico Higuain has been fired for cause, effective immediately, in the wake of his suspension by MLS NEXT Pro following an incident of misconduct towards a female referee.
stories.body:
The Columbus Crew announced that Crew 2 manager Federico Higuain has been fired for cause, effective immediately, in the wake of his suspension by MLS NEXT Pro following an incident of misconduct towards a female referee.

"We determined it's in the best interest of our Club, players and support staff to dismiss Federico Higuaín from his responsibilities," said Crew General Manager Issa Tall in prepared statement. "After conversations this week and further assessing the past month, our Club's standards of what's expected from a leader for one of our teams have not been met," The Crew's statement added that for the 2026 MLS NEXT Pro Playoffs, the Crew 2 technical staff will assume additional responsibilities ahead of the Club's search for a full-time head coach for the side.

Higuain, 41, was suspended for two games following an Aug. 23 incident that involved him refusing to let go of the hand of a female referee during the post-game handshake, despite being asked three times to do so. Higuain also directed a sexist remark toward the referee saying: "Don't forget that this is a man's game."

Higuain, who excelled as a player for the Crew over eight seasons, was red carded for the incident. In addition to the two-game suspension, Higuain was ordered to undergo restorative practice training, sources told ESPN.

An MLS NEXT Pro spokesperson confirmed that Higuain was suspended for just one additional game, as the policy allows for the red card to count towards the total suspension. The same spokesperson wasn't able to answer the question of why Higuain's actions didn't constitute a forceful grab.

The Professional Soccer Referees Association (PSRA), the union that represents MLS and USL referees, brought the incident to light over the weekend, stating in a social media post that it was not satisfied with the penalties, adding that a "forceful grab" plus the discriminatory language should have been penalized more severely.

While the PSRA's post didn't mention Higuain by name, ESPN reported that the coach in question was Higuain.

"The League's response falls drastically short of the right message to the participants, the referees, and the public. It needs to be reevaluated," the PSRA's social media post read.

The Crew initially issued a statement stating that, "The Crew actively collaborated with MLS NEXT Pro throughout the review process and fully accepted the additional discipline issued in accordance with league policies.

"We condemn any action or notion that contradicts our mission of uniting and uplifting all communities and genders through the global game."

But sources with knowledge of the Crew's decision to fire its coach told ESPN that the club wasn't satisfied with Higuain's response to the incident, saying there was a "lack of contrition" on his part, that he refused to issue a public apology to the female referee, and that there was an overall lack of accountability on the part of its second-team coach.

There was pressure from several of the Crew's supporters groups as well, including the Nordecke and CapyBrava, which both made social media posts demanding that Higuain be fired.

One source said that Higuain was informed of the club's decision early Tuesday afternoon.

In a statement given to ESPN on Sunday, MLS NEXT Pro said the league "immediately investigated the reported incident between the head coach and the female official. It was determined that the coach's behavior violated League policies and warranted additional discipline beyond the red card that was issued in the moment. He served a two-game suspension and is required to participate in a multi-session restorative practices process, which is already underway. The program is intended to support the League's efforts to foster understanding, accountability, respect, and the restoration of relationships across the League. MLS NEXT Pro believes in the restorative approach. The League is confident in its process and the results."

stories.headline: Still at zero: Viral Man United fan's haircut challenge nears two years
stories.summary: Viral Manchester United fan Frank Ilett's haircut challenge is nearing the two-year mark and he's back to square 1.
stories.body:
For most clubs, failure or success can be defined in points, trophies and medals. Manchester United are the same, but they can also define it in days. More specifically, it can be summed up in 712 days.

That's how long viral United fan Frank Ilett, also known as The United Strand, has gone without a haircut as he waits for the team to win five games in a row.

After finishing last season with wins over Nottingham Forest and Brighton, Michael Carrick's side could have completed the job with wins over newly promoted Hull City and Ipswich Town before finishing with a win away at Everton. As it turned out, that's not at all what happened.

An embarrassing 2-0 away defeat to Hull meant going back to square one. A 5-2 win over Ipswich might have promoted hopes that the season opener was just an unwanted blip, but a draw to Everton and a controversial defeat to 10-man Manchester City poured further cold water.

How could it get worse? Well, a 2-0 lead inside the first 10 minutes against Brighton in the Carabao Cup ended in a surprise 3-2 defeat.

Left watching on, his hair growing ever longer, is Ilett. His challenge will now officially reach the two-year mark -- his last haircut was on Oct. 5, 2024 -- and his hair is now almost 14 inches at its longest point.

In the meantime, Ilett continues to raise money for the Little Princess Trust, which creates wigs for children with cancer.

The only thing that can happen now before Ilett soars past two years is for United to win away to Fulham in their last game before the international break.

This is it, the weekend when we decide the two teams that will battle it out for the 2026 NRL premiership, and we have been presented with two cracking games to determine the grand finalists. Prediction: The Dolphins were very impressive two weeks ago against the Warriors, restricting them to one try, before unleashing their signature attacking blitz after the break. Previously this season they have allowed teams to get away to big head starts before mounting their fightback, a ploy which just won't stand up in the finals. They appear to have taken note and their defensive work in New Zealand was outstanding. They will need to be at their very best once more against the Roosters, who have the attacking flair to cause them plenty of problems.

The Roosters were simply too good for the Sharks last week, after going very close to beating the Panthers the week before. They have plenty of experience across the park, with Daly Cherry-Evans putting in a much better performance against the Sharks in combination with the hard running Hugo Savala. Outside those two, the Roosters backline bristles with attacking weapons, with Robert Toia and Mark Nawaqanitawase in unstoppable form, James Tedesco always lurking, and Sam Walker returning at halfback.

But, as we all know, the backs don't win the big games, they just determine the score, and the Roosters have a pack that is the match of any in the league. Naufahu Whyte, Lindsay Collins and Siua Wong were at their destructive best against the Sharks. stories.headline: NBA Rank 2026: Snubs, surprises and reaction from insiders
stories.summary: Did LeBron, Steph and KD rank right? NBA insiders breakdown their biggest snubs, surprises and predictions from this year's rank.
stories.body:
ESPN continues its countdown of the top 100 players entering the 2026-27 NBA season after rolling out 50-11 today and 100-51 on Monday.

LeBron James, Stephen Curry and Kevin Durant continue their reign near the top of NBA rank as some of the longest-tenured players in the league. But what new faces made their debut?

Before we reveal the top 10 best players in the league, our expert panel breaks down this year's list, answering the biggest questions on surprise snubs and who's up next to break through the rankings.

LeBron James' No. 18 ranking is _____.

Jamal Collier: Questionable. What's the argument for LeBron still being ranked several spots behind the other "old guys" of his generation -- Curry, Durant or Kawhi Leonard?

LeBron carried the Los Angeles Lakers to a playoff series win last year with Luka Doncic injured and Austin Reaves out for most of the series against the Houston Rockets. Injured or not, Durant hasn't won a playoff series since 2023. Curry is still the engine for the Golden State Warriors but didn't get out of the play-in tournament and has played fewer games than LeBron. Leonard is coming off one of the best regular seasons of his career, but he's far from reliable from a health perspective.

LeBron transitioned into a new role with the Lakers and, after an adjustment period, excelled. It might take some time for everyone to adjust in Philly, but James has continued to be as consistent a bet as nearly everyone ahead of him.

Tim MacMahon: Fair. At the ripe age of 41, he's still a legitimate All-Star, which is an unprecedented feat in NBA history. But James is a cut below All-NBA-caliber at this point in his legendary career. He's no longer capable of being the best player on a championship contender, but there has never been a better bargain on a veterans minimum contract.

Anthony Slater: A hint at both the talent glut and offensive challenges ahead for the Sixers. James is behind two of his younger teammates in this rank. Tyrese Maxey (No. 11) is exploding into his prime, and Jaylen Brown (No. 14) is coming off a top-six MVP finish. James had to rearrange his game to take a supplementary role last season next to Doncic and Reaves (when both were healthy). Finding that sweet spot when sharing the floor with Maxey and Brown will define Philadelphia's season.

Brian Windhorst: Appropriate. After the All-Star break last season, LeBron shot 54% and averaged seven rebounds and seven assists while having the lowest usage rate of his career. He morphed midyear into one of the best transition scorers in the league and an off-ball cutter. Had he played five more games and gotten to 65, he very well could have made the All-NBA team.

Which player's ranking surprised you the most?

Collier: Tyrese Haliburton at No. 19 is too low. Haliburton played like a top 10 player during the 2025 playoffs, and he has had more than enough time to recover from an Achilles tear. His regular-season stats might not be as gaudy as some of the guys ahead of him on this list, but his past two seasons have ended in the Eastern Conference finals. I'm not ready to underestimate him again.

MacMahon: Walker Kessler managed to move up 25 spots from last year's rankings after playing a total of five games last season. Such is the benefit of the Lakers limelight, I guess. An argument could be made that Kessler will improve significantly simply by playing alongside Doncic, the league's premier pick-and-roll creator. But it's on Kessler to prove the Lakers made a wise move by paying so much -- in draft capital and dollars -- to bring him to Los Angeles. Our panel is giving him the benefit of the doubt.

Slater: Jaden McDaniels. I covered Minnesota's first-round series win over the Denver Nuggets. McDaniels, without Anthony Edwards, closed it down in Game 6 with 32 points while holding Jamal Murray to 4-for-17 shooting. It capped one of the best trash-talking two-way series performances in recent memory from a young wing. Murray couldn't do anything against McDaniels for two weeks, and his offense took a leap. McDaniels is No. 56, and Julius Randle is No. 54. The Timberwolves just traded one to generate more room for the other. You could make a coherent argument that McDaniels should be ranked higher than players all the way up into the early 30s.

Windhorst: Scottie Barnes at No. 17. Solely based on last season, this is a fair spot for him, however, this positioning underrates him looking forward, which is the point of this list. He has grown into one of the best two-way players in the league and was an absolute force for Toronto last season. With Leonard arriving to support him, he has a chance to be a top 10 guy this season.

Which player outside the top 25 will get there next season?

Collier: I'd look to this year's rookie class. A lot of talent just came into the league through the draft, especially among the top four picks. AJ Dybantsa or Darryn Peterson might be the easiest bet to rise into these ranks, similar to how Cooper Flagg went from No. 52 last year to No. 23 entering this season. Someone from this incoming class is bound to arrive All-Star ready.

MacMahon: Stephon Castle moved up 61 spots since last year and could make another leap, especially if he continues to improve as a 3-point shooter. He made significant statistical improvement across the board in his sophomore NBA season, averaging 16.7 points, 5.3 rebounds and 7.4 assists. An All-Star berth and All-Defensive Team selection are reasonable goals for Castle this season.

Slater: I'm going to cheat slightly and discuss the player ranked No. 25. Jalen Williams is primed to reclaim a place higher on this list. He dropped from No. 11 last season after missing 49 games and a chunk of the Thunder's playoff run because of persistent injuries. But the word is that he has had a laser-focused summer attempting to correct his issues. At 23 years old, he was an All-NBA second teamer, an All-NBA defender and a fringe top-10 player. Now, he's 25 and more than capable of rediscovering that form if he can stay healthy.

Windhorst: Dylan Harper is a quiet storm. He was probably the Spurs' second-best player down the stretch last season. He's a bit undervalued because he came off the bench, but I believe in Year 2 he'll be unleashed and getting way more attention from opposing teams.

Which player on a new team will most outperform their ranking?

Collier: I like the potential that LaMelo Ball could sneak into the top 25. There's a lot of upside if he can build off last season in his transition to the Minnesota Timberwolves and continue to be a winning player. The Wolves haven't ever put a point guard with this much potential next to Anthony Edwards, and it could unlock something for both players if all goes well.

MacMahon: At 27 years old, Jaren Jackson Jr. should be entering his prime. He has proved that he can average 20-plus points per game and dominate defensively. That's why the Utah Jazz gave up a bundle of first-round picks to get him last season. That two-way impact would make Jackson much better than the 53rd-best player in the league. He was No. 31 in last year's rankings and is likely to return to that range.

Slater: I'll go way off the board and take a stab at an unranked late lottery rookie: Yaxel Lendeborg. Looking at the Warriors roster, Curry is their only player ranked in the top 90, and he missed half of last season. Jimmy Butler III probably won't appear until the new year. They ache for talent. Steve Kerr has already hinted that a path to a starting role and major minutes awaits for Lendeborg, if he can seize it. He's an older rookie, turning 24 later this month but already has the strength and size of a midprime wing. If he can burst onto the scene and help drag the Warriors to a better-than-expected record, he will quickly vault into these types of conversations.

Windhorst: Anthony Davis is highly incentivized to have a massive season, and the Washington Wizards, even though they are not going to extend his contract right now, are invested in him doing so. Obviously, his health is the X factor, and counting on him is dangerous. But he's not the 40th-best player in the league when he's active and healthy.

The top three was one of the closest races in NBA Rank history. What's your prediction?

Collier: It's easy to see why Victor Wembanyama will be in position to take the No.1 spot after his impressive Finals run, but Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's consistency might be a bit overlooked at this point. He's the best offensive engine in the league, hits consistent 30-point games and despite injuries and a disappointing series from Chet Holmgren, he carried the Thunder through the postseason. He shouldn't be unseated lightly. But the potential for an even greater level up from Wembanyama this season is too tantalizing to ignore.

MacMahon: Is it premature to anoint Wemby as the league's best player? Perhaps, given that he has yet to hoist an MVP or championship trophy. But he'd get my vote, just ahead of SGA and Nikola Jokic.

Slater: Wembanyama in the top slot because he conquered the Thunder in the conference finals. Gilgeous-Alexander in the second slot because of his back-to-back MVPs. Jokic in the third slot and perhaps with a little chip on his shoulder to reclaim both his and the Nuggets' place at the top of the NBA mountain.

Windhorst: In this group there's a two-time reigning MVP in his prime, and history suggests that this player would enter the following season regarded as the league's No. 1. But something tells me that SGA won't be No. 1, and for him it'll be nothing but motivation. I would guess that Wembanyama takes that pedestal, and he plainly believes he is No. 1. But the guy who was No. 1 when it mattered most last season currently plays in New York, so let's see where this panel placed Jalen Brunson.

BONUS! Make a bold prediction for any player in ESPN's top 100

Collier: Detroit Pistons' Ausar Thompson will make a leap on this list next year. He's already up to No. 59 after not being ranked the previous year. He has offensive limitations, but he's almost certainly the best perimeter defender in the league right now. Thompson terrorized the Cleveland Cavaliers during last season's playoffs, so much that coach Kenny Atkinson revealed one of their adjustments was "throw the ball wherever Thompson isn't." If Thompson can improve his jump shot and finishing around the rim, he'll certainly reach that next level. But still, being a lockdown defender with assignments against the best wings in the league is going to earn Thompson a nice living

MacMahon: At least five top 100 players will be wearing different uniforms after the trade deadline. That list will include at least two of our top 40.

Slater: The stage is set for Cason Wallace's breakout season. He is respectably ranked No. 75, considering he has been mostly a lower-usage defensive ace for the Oklahoma City Thunder his first few seasons. But the Luguentz Dort trade cleared the way for him to claim a permanent starting slot, and he appears more than ready to leap into the next stage of his career right as he is due for an extension.

Windhorst: I don't make predictions, but I will say that throughout all last season, Cooper Flagg kept giving me flashbacks to LeBron James as a rookie. By LeBron's second season, he was a top-five player, and I feel strongly that this is Flagg's destiny too. We'll just have to wait and see how fast that prophecy is fulfilled.

stories.headline: Fantasy football consistency ratings: 2024 to 2026
stories.summary: The consistency ratings weigh both how consistent and how start-worthy players have been from 2024 to 2026.
stories.body:
Updated Sept. 22, 2026 (through Week 2 of 2026)

How consistency ratings work
Using fantasy points determined by ESPN's standard scoring, the charts contained in this column rate players based upon how consistently reliable they have been during the 2024 through 2026 seasons, a span of 38 weeks' worth of games (18 weeks apiece in 2024 and 2025, two so far in 2026). For IDPs (individual defensive players), the scoring from our weekly rankings is used: solo tackle (1.5), assisted tackle (0.75), tackle for loss (2), sack (4), interception (5), forced fumble (4), fumble recovery (4), touchdown (6), safety (2), pass defended (1.5). To familiarize you with the terminology and column headers listed in the charts below:

Start%: The player's "start percentage," which shows how often he earned a start in an ESPN standard PPR (points per reception) league. This is his number of "starts" -- those defined below -- divided by his number of scheduled team games.

CR: The player's "consistency rating," which is calculated as his weekly standard deviation divided by his PPR fantasy points per game average. This is meant to identify the players who were most consistently close to their weekly averages. The lower the number, the more consistent the player. Again, lower numbers are better.

nPPR%: The player's start percentage using non-PPR scoring, using ESPN's standard scoring settings without any points per reception.

FPTS/G: The player's average PPR fantasy points scored per game.

Start: The number of times that the player's point total in a given week was worthy of having had him active in an ESPN standard PPR league.

Star: The number of times the player's point total ranked among the best at his position.

Stiff: The number of times the player's point total ranked among the worst at his position, making almost any waiver-wire option a smarter choice.

These are the benchmarks for what constitutes a "start," "star" or "stiff" performance:

Sat: The number of times the player sat out a game. Players are not charged "stiff" points for sitting out, nor does it impact their overall consistency rating (CR), but it hurts their overall start percentage.

Players must have a start rate of at least 20% in either standard PPR or non-PPR scoring, rank among the top 20 quarterbacks, tight ends or kickers, top 50 running backs or wide receivers, or top 40 defensive linemen, linebackers or defensive backs, in terms of total fantasy points at their position from 2023 to 2025, or are averaging at least 50 snaps per game, for inclusion in the chart. stories.headline: Full final 2026 regular-season grades for all 30 MLB teams
stories.summary: Whether your team is headed to October or packing its bags for the offseason, how did 2026 measure up to expectations?
stories.body:
As we wrap up the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season, it's time for some final grades.

As expected, the Los Angeles Dodgers challenged the single-season record for wins. The New York Mets had a huge offseason that paid off with the National League East title. The New York Yankees dominated the American League East. The Milwaukee Brewers failed to scrap their way to the playoffs. Tarik Skubal carried the Detroit Tigers to the AL Central championship. The Chicago White Sox? A joke once again.

Wait ... no, that's not at all what happened. The only joke -- outside of the usual ineptitude we see from the clubs at the bottom of the majors -- was the AL West, which might see a team with a losing record capture the division title.

The 2026 season might not have gone as expected, but we still had breakout performances, surprising teams, unpredictable results, a flamethrowing phenom, a season for the ages and a very mediocre AL. Let's go to the grades.

Milwaukee Brewers: A+

What a wonderful, engaging and thrilling regular season for the Brewers. They've already set the franchise record for wins in a single season, breaking last year's mark of 97, and are heading to the top record in the majors for the second year in a row. Jacob Misiorowski has been the best individual story of the season -- alongside division rival Pete Crow-Armstrong -- but it has been an impressive teamwide effort.

Milwaukee's rookie pitchers have started 77 games, most in the majors, while another pair of rookies in shortstop Cooper Pratt and right fielder Luis Lara will be starting in October. Brice Turang's 6.9 bWAR is second among MLB position players, and he should finish in the top five of the MVP voting. Oh, and the bullpen is top five in the majors in win probability added.

Not bad for a team that was 11th in ESPN's preseason power rankings. At least we got "the thing we'll be talking about most this season" right for Milwaukee: Misiorowski's sophomore year.

Tampa Bay Rays: A+

Nope, the Rays never faded. In fact, they went 18-10 in August and are 14-6 in September after clinching the division (and the top record in the AL) with a win over the Yankees on Tuesday.

Tampa Bay has been a little hard to analyze at times as it has gone 25-14 in one-run games, which helps erase its 22-23 record in blowout games decided by five-plus. (Good teams almost always have a winning record in blowout games, so this is a weird anomaly.) While Junior Caminero has been a standout and Jonathan Aranda is closing in on 100 RBIs, it's been a year of unsung heroes: Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen lead the rotation with 15 wins apiece and sub 3.00 ERAs; Griffin Jax transitioned from reliever to starter; Bryan Baker leads the majors in saves; Victor Mesa Jr. added surprising power in the second half.

You can ask the same question about the Brewers and the Rays: Will this be the year?

Atlanta Braves: A

More steady than dominant, the Braves built an early lead in the NL East but appeared vulnerable at times to the Phillies catching them -- a lead that was as large as 10½ games on May 22 got as low as two games -- but Atlanta beat Philadelphia four out of seven games in September to essentially wrap up the division.

Huge shoutout to Chris Sale, who carried a rotation that received just eight starts from Spencer Strider and none from Spencer Schwellenbach. Grant Holmes and Martin Perez also stepped up, while trade addition Tyler Mahle has been the best pickup of the deadline. Alongside Sale, the bullpen has been the team's MVP, with the highest win probability added in the majors.

Chicago White Sox: A

We're keeping this an "A" for now, although if the White Sox can rally over these final few days and win the division, it should bump up to an "A+" as one of the least likely division titles in recent memory. Preseason forecasts: 61-101 on ESPN, 67-95 on FanGraphs. Instead, with Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery each topping 30 home runs, the White Sox have slugged their way -- hopefully -- into the playoffs, even if it's just a wild card.

They got just enough pitching, especially from a bullpen that has pitched the most innings in the majors (and is wearing that a bit down the stretch here). Heck, Tristan Peters went from former Savannah Banana to AL All-Star. What's not to love about this season?

Los Angeles Dodgers: B+

For most teams, closing in on 100 wins is an easy "A" grade. For the Dodgers, that's called meeting expectations. True, they might get there even though Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell have combined for just 20 starts and Shohei Ohtani didn't pitch again after early July, finishing with a 1.79 ERA in 14 starts. But still, nobody feels sorry for them. Those various pitching injury concerns led to the Skubal trade.

So, the concerns have now shifted to an offense that scuffled at times in the second half -- although it has averaged 5.7 runs per game during the current 15-3 stretch. Even Kyle Tucker is suddenly red hot, with six home runs and a .641 slugging percentage in September. That stretch came against non-playoff teams with bad pitching, though -- the Dodgers are just 18-18 against the five other NL playoff teams.

Nonetheless, with Skubal, Snell pitching well and Yoshinobu Yamamoto as good as ever, the Dodgers might be peaking at the right time.

San Diego Padres: B+

It's been a roller coaster of a season for the Padres, who are playing their best baseball heading into October. They got off to a strong start that saw them 29-18 on May 18 and in first place in the division -- even though Fernando Tatis Jr. hadn't homered, Manny Machado was hitting .180 and Jackson Merrill was hitting .202. Remarkably, Tatis didn't homer until his 56th game but is now up to 25.

By July 23, however, the Padres were 50-53, but they won eight of nine just before the trade deadline and general manager A.J. Preller boosted the rotation with Casey Mize and Robbie Ray. Those two haven't actually pitched well, but the resurgent offense has helped them match the Rays for the best record since the deadline. With Tatis and Merrill on fire, Ty France having a huge season and Mason Miller ready to lock things down in the ninth inning, maybe this is the Padres team that gets to the World Series.

New York Yankees: B+

General manager Brian Cashman has been much maligned by Yankees fans in recent years for failing to build a World Series winner, but the depth of the roster he built has once again carried the team to the postseason. Even with Aaron Judge missing more than 90 games, the Yankees are still neck and neck with the Cubs for most home runs in the majors. Despite Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon missing significant time, they lead the majors in rotation ERA.

Two relievers Cashman picked up off the scrap pile of free talent, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick, are a key reason the Yankees are second in bullpen ERA. Then there's Cam Schlittler, who burst onto the scene last year and has now turned into a sure-thing Cy Young winner. Judge's right calf strain, which put him back on the IL -- the reason he's not expected to play in the wild-card series -- is a big worry, but maybe the Yankees can pitch-and-defense their way to their first World Series championship since 2009.

Boston Red Sox: B

The Red Sox are a playoff team, which isn't necessarily a surprise, but it's a huge surprise given they were 32-46 on June 24 and chief baseball officer Craig Breslow appeared like he might be joining manager Alex Cora on the unemployment line. Soon after, a 9-0 road trip turned into a 15-game winning streak, part of a remarkable 32-5 stretch -- and they did that without Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony, their projected two best players.

A bunch of unsung role players -- such as Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper and Jake Bennett -- have contributed, as has a bullpen that leads the majors in ERA and outfielders Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela, who have each posted 5-WAR seasons. Breslow went all-in to acquire Adley Rutschman at the deadline, giving up three top-10 prospects, but Rutschman has hit .214/.270/.398 in 28 games with the Red Sox.

The "win now" nature of that trade means the Red Sox aren't really underdogs, even if they're painted as such -- and they'll have to beat the Yankees and Rays just to reach the American League Championship Series.

Cleveland Guardians: B

No doubt, there's a little "right division, right time" going on for the Guardians, but while the Tigers underachieved, and the Twins couldn't put it all together, and the Royals stumbled around all season ... well, none of that ever happens to the Guardians, does it? They always reach their level.

That's mostly because the pitching is usually good and sometimes great. They're the only team with four starters with at least 30 starts (no other team has more than two), and then they added Foster Griffin at the trade deadline. The offense has been much better in the second half with Steven Kwan getting on base at around a .400 clip, which sort of gets everything going. Rookies Chase DeLauter and Travis Bazzana rank 1-2 on the team in OPS+. Throw in team MVP Parker Messick -- he's 12-9 with a 2.57 ERA -- and this might be the best rookie class in franchise history.

Chicago Cubs: B

The goal was a division title -- which has eluded the Cubs in a full season since 2017 -- so finishing in second place for a fourth consecutive season, and not especially close to the Brewers either, is a bit anticlimactic. Thanks to Crow-Armstrong and the majors' leading offense, however, it was an entertaining season -- and the Cubs are at least headed to the playoffs barring a last-week collapse. PCA's 10.4 FanGraphs WAR is the second highest by a position player in franchise history (behind Rogers Hornsby's 11.0 WAR in 1929). That's the stat of the year for the Cubs -- followed by the 14 different relievers who have recorded a save (tied for second most in MLB history).

Miami Marlins: B

The Marlins are going to finish with about the same record as last season, but this was a much better club. The 2025 squad went 79-83 but had a minus-89 run differential. Sitting at plus-3 with a few games remaining, this year's Marlins might finish with a positive run differential for the first time since -- drum roll, please -- 2010. Ouch.

Miami's top takeaway of 2026 was the double-play combo of Otto Lopez and Xavier Edwards. While both faded at the plate in the second half, they still combined for 9 WAR, giving the Marlins their best middle infield since the heyday of Hanley Ramirez and Dan Uggla. Max Meyer made the All-Star team before finishing on the injured list with a neck injury, and Eury Perez flashed his top-of-the-rotation stuff (and mid-rotation inconsistency). Unfortunately, pitching prospects Thomas White (shoulder) and Robby Snelling (Tommy John surgery) were unable to impact the major league team as expected heading into the season.

Washington Nationals: B

The Nationals are probably going to finish third in the majors in runs scored, which nobody would have predicted heading into the season -- and they're doing it with the youngest group of position players in the league, per Baseball-Reference. President of baseball operations Paul Toboni did cash in on Luis Garcia Jr. and Curtis Mead at the trade deadline, so the offense has been only middle-of-the-pack since then, but it's a promising turnaround for a moribund franchise.

Has any player changed his game as much as CJ Abrams? When he came up with the Padres in 2022, he was a skinny, slap-hitting 21-year-old with no power -- he ranked 262nd out of 281 position players in average exit velocity. Fast-forward to 2026 and he has hit 31 home runs. Now get Abrams and James Wood some pitching help.

Philadelphia Phillies: B-

Few teams have kept their core group in place for as many years as the Phillies -- Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Bryson Stott and Alec Bohm have all been regulars since 2022, with Trea Turner joining the team in 2023 -- and it looks likely to result in a fifth consecutive playoff appearance. It hasn't been an easy season though.

Manager Rob Thomson got fired. The Phillies ceded the NL East title back to the Braves for the first time since 2023. The offense is mediocre (14th overall in runs, including 24th on the road). The defense, especially in the first half, was terrible. And now Jesus Luzardo, the team's best starter the past two months, is injured with his playoff status up in the air. At least Aaron Nola is pitching his best baseball in a couple of years. Given the age of this team, it's World Series or bust one more time.

Pittsburgh Pirates: B-

What a fascinating yet ultimately frustrating season for the Pirates. They made a basically impossible improvement on offense, jumping from last in the majors in runs to fifth. Brandon Lowe led the way, but it was a deep lineup, with 20-year-old rookie Konnor Griffin showing why he projects as a future star. The aggravating part comes with Paul Skenes' 3.91 ERA -- he recently said pitching in the World Baseball Classic was the "root" of his issues -- and Mitch Keller's 5.29 ERA in 22 starts. With better results from those two, maybe the Pirates make the playoffs for the first time since 2015.

Arizona Diamondbacks: C+

The Diamondbacks somehow hung in the wild-card race all the way until the final week of the season, even though their core group -- Corbin Carroll, Geraldo Perdomo, Ketel Marte, Merrill Kelly and Zac Gallen -- have all had better seasons. Carroll was the best of the group and Perdomo came on in the second half, but Kelly and Gallen are 12-23 with minus-1.4 WAR and Marte had another mysterious absence this year.

Others stepped up -- Gabriel Moreno should finish in the top 10 of the MVP voting and Eduardo Rodriguez will receive some down-ballot MVP votes, while the bullpen was shockingly one of the best in baseball -- but the Diamondbacks need to figure out how to build a 95-win team instead of an 85-win one. We'll see if general manager Mike Hazen and skipper Torey Lovullo will remain around to do that.

Texas Rangers: C

The Rangers have hovered between six games under .500 (the low point on May 28) and three games over .500 (the high point on July 28) all season. Thanks to their division, they've never been more than three games out of first and entered this final week one game ahead of the Astros. The team MVPs have been utility guy Ezequiel Duran and closer Jacob Latz. That feels like the very definition of a "C" grade. The Rangers have struggled to score runs all season and, no, that's not just Globe Life Field: They're 23rd in runs per game at home and 25th on the road. They don't even have an ace, as Jacob deGrom has been their best starter and he's 11-10 with a 3.86 ERA. Despite all of that, they might luck into a division title anyway.

Houston Astros: C

As is the case with the Rangers, this mark can go up or down a half grade based on the final standings -- but regardless of the final outcome, this is the worst Astros team since 2014, the final losing season before the rebirth began in 2015. Owner Jim Crane certainly isn't happy with how the season has gone, firing general manager Dana Brown in late August with manager Joe Espada likely to go as well when his contract expires after the season.

Was Crane right to expect more? Not really. Houston was 13th in ESPN's preseason power rankings with a projected record of 84-78. FanGraphs saw the Astros as the third-best team in the AL West, predicting an 80-82 record. They are what was expected: a flawed, top-heavy roster with thin depth on the pitching staff. That's how it played out.

And -- stop me if this sounds familiar -- they might luck into a division title anyway.

St. Louis Cardinals: C

The Cardinals weren't a disaster in 2026, which is a good thing, considering this team could have easily gone sideways. Chaim Bloom, in his first year heading up baseball operations, completely committed to youth, running out the second-youngest group of position players in the majors.

Jordan Walker finally broke out and Alec Burleson is leading the majors in RBIs, which no Cardinals player has done since Joe Torre in 1971. JJ Wetherholt showed he's going to be a valuable player; he and Masyn Winn might both win Gold Gloves. There is more young talent on the way, too, with Leo Bernal and Joshua Baez getting a taste of the big leagues this season, and Rainiel Rodriguez, Liam Doyle and Tanner Franklin next in line.

The best thing here is that the Cardinals were at least interesting for the first time in a long time. (Even some of their recent playoff teams weren't all that exciting.) The payroll has been trimmed to the bare bones, so there's room heading into 2027 to address the rotation and bullpen.

Minnesota Twins: C-

Minnesota was close in the division race until fading -- once again -- over the final two months, a period in which Byron Buxton played just 11 games and Joe Ryan made just four starts. (The Twins lost all four.) What this franchise needs more than anything is some star power. Maybe late-season call-ups Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez will eventually be those guys. Or shortstop Kaelen Culpepper, who looked promising in the 25 games he played before getting injured. Taj Bradley did have a superb season, and rotation mates Zebby Matthews and rookie Connor Prielipp also flashed some good stuff at times. There's a potentially nice foundation brewing here, but keep in mind: The Twins' Opening Day payroll was their lowest since 2014. If only ownership were a little more committed to winning.

Baltimore Orioles: C-

Meh. I mean, you could say that about the entire AL, but the Orioles were especially "meh" in 2026. OK, Pete Alonso was fun, although the most fun he had was his return to Citi Field last week. Whatever happened to Gunnar Henderson is one of the biggest mysteries of the entire 2026 season. Any hope for the Orioles in 2027 rests on him returning to superstar status. Jackson Holliday? Still young, but his star has dimmed. Rutschman? Gone. Samuel Basallo? Promising, maybe fun. The story of the 2023-to-2026 Orioles is this: You never know what the future is going to bring. Go for it when you can. And if you have a new owner who promises he wants to win, don't believe it until he shows it.

Detroit Tigers: D+

It might be easy to blame the bullpen here, as despite a plus-73 in run differential -- best in the division and fourth best in the AL (and just a few runs behind the Rays and Red Sox) -- Detroit's 15-27 record in one-run games dragged down its overall record. But let's focus on something else.

The Tigers went 3-10 against the Guardians and 4-9 against the White Sox, averaging just 3.3 runs per game in those 26 contests. That's not going to work, even if Mariano Rivera is your closer. Despite a nice run in June and July when they went 30-20, the Tigers decided to punt at the deadline and traded Skubal. They played well immediately after the trade and got to 2½ games out of the division lead before a 3-14 stretch buried them. With Skubal done and dusted, president of baseball operations Scott Harris will need to take a deep look at where the Tigers stand: Since last Aug. 24, they are 83-106.

Colorado Rockies: D+

The Rockies will finish with a fourth straight 100-loss season and likely the worst record in the majors, but this was still a major step forward from 2025, as their run differential improved from minus-424 (the worst in modern MLB history) to minus-177 (not even the worst in 2026).

Most of the strides came on offense, as the Rockies improved from last in the majors in runs per game on the road to 21st, as the first year of the Paul DePodesta/Josh Byrnes-led front office unearthed a 3.5-WAR player from the Yankees in TJ Rumfield and saw another big season from Hunter Goodman, plus promising returns from farm system prospects Kyle Karros and Cole Carrigg. The pitching remains a mess, and you can't give a 100-loss team a grade higher than a D+, but as DePodesta and Byrnes work to modernize the organization, the Rockies might be headed in the right direction.

Toronto Blue Jays: D

It has obviously been a disappointing follow-up to Toronto's World Series appearance last year, so it's fair to ask: Was 2025 just a fluke? The Blue Jays were 74-88 in 2024, 94-68 in 2025 and 77-80 so far in 2026. The outlier was an offensive surge in 2025 compared with the other two seasons -- and it's not all on Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s shoulders, with the Jays on pace to score 145 fewer runs in 2026 than last year. Guerrero is responsible for about 41 runs of that decline, or about 28%. That leaves 72% for the front office to figure out how to fix for next season.

Kansas City Royals: D

The path to nowhere for the Royals was set early when Bobby Witt Jr. somehow scored just one run in the team's first 18 games. He then scored three runs in a game -- but then went six more runless games and didn't hit a home run until his 29th game. This isn't on Witt, as he's likely to get some first-place MVP votes since he leads AL position players in FanGraphs WAR, but it's an example of how the Royals just never got in sync all season. They had just one winning month, in August, and they especially struggled against good teams, going a wretched 7-24 against the AL East and 19-29 against the NL. After back-to-back winning seasons, it was a disappointing flop, leaving Kansas City with a lot of holes to fix.

Cincinnati Reds: D

After making the playoffs in 2025, only the A's and Rockies are going to end up with a worse run differential than the Reds. Somehow, they have Elly De La Cruz, probable NL Rookie of the Year Sal Stewart and Chase Burns, who went 15-3 with a 2.86 ERA and 185 strikeouts, and yet still ended up as a dreary watch -- especially disappointing considering they were 20-11 at the end of April. Blame the rotation. After ranking 16th in the majors in rotation ERA in 2024 and an impressive ninth (considering its bandbox of a home park) in 2025, Cincinnati fell to 28th in 2026 despite Burns' excellence.

It feels like the Reds need an identity. They're not a pitching-and-defense team. (The defense was bad.) They have the veneer of a power-hitting team, at least in 2026, but the park helps inflate their power totals. They don't hit for average (last in the majors). If they're going to build around pitching, maybe it makes sense to change the dimensions of the park and get some better defenders to surround De La Cruz and Stewart.

Athletics: D-

The A's can at least use injuries as an excuse for going backward from 2025, as Nick Kurtz, Brent Rooker, Shea Langeliers, Jacob Wilson and Tyler Soderstrom all missed significant time. Indeed, they were hovering around .500 in late May -- which meant they were in first place in the AL West -- until all the injuries became too much. They've been the worst team in the majors since July 1. Rooker and Wilson didn't hit when they played, and Lawrence Butler spent the first half hitting like Craig Paquette's long-lost cousin. It's easy to point fingers at the pitching staff -- the A's have allowed nearly 100 more runs than any non-Rockies team -- but some of that is playing in Sacramento, as the A's have a lower road ERA than AL West rivals Seattle, Houston and Texas.

New York Mets: D-

A reminder: ESPN ranked the Mets sixth in its preseason Power Rankings with a projected record of 92-70 and 78% playoff odds. FanGraphs had the Mets as the NL East favorites with a 38% chance of winning the division, just ahead of the Braves, and an 80% chance of making the playoffs. On paper, it did look like a good team, so the playoff expectations were absolutely realistic. We all know what happened: injuries, poor performance, Alonso leading the league in RBIs ... for the Orioles. Oops.

What keeps the Mets from receiving a failing grade, however, is they at least have been respectable under interim manager Andy Green -- so much so that the interim tag was removed and Green was hired to a three-year deal on Tuesday -- and rookies Nolan McLean, Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing have performed well, providing a much-needed influx of young talent. Still, president of baseball operations David Stearns is on the hot seat to improve this club for 2027 after his 2025-26 offseason (signing Bo Bichette, Jorge Polanco, Marcus Semien, Freddy Peralta, Luis Robert Jr. and Devin Williams) goes down as one of the worst ever.

Los Angeles Angels: F

The Angels set a franchise record with 99 losses in 2024, and with 97 losses so far, this team may surpass that mark, so we're pretty much stuck giving them a failing grade. If you're counting, that's 11 consecutive losing seasons and 12 consecutive non-playoff seasons. The best news came in early September when Arte Moreno agreed to sell the team for $4 billion to Stan Kroenke, owner of the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche, Arsenal F.C. and other sports franchises. On the field, there were -- believe it or not -- some interesting developments, especially Walbert Urena and Reid Detmers in the rotation, part of a group that has the second-best ERA since the beginning of August.

San Francisco Giants: F

It's fair to say the first year of the Tony Vitello managerial era played out with all the fervor of fireworks on a rain-drenched Fourth of July. Did he get the most out of this team? No. Is the team's second 90-loss season since 2008 his fault? Also no. President of baseball operations Buster Posey has voiced his support, so Vitello will likely return for 2027, which puts the pressure on Posey to figure this out.

The biggest problem here: Rafael Devers, while rebounding from a terrible start to have a productive season, is signed for seven more years and $223 million; Willy Adames is owed $155.5 million for five years; Matt Chapman, just over $100 million for four years; and Jung Hoo Lee, $65 million for three. That's a lot of money for a group that combined for less than 10 WAR. While Bryce Eldridge had a promising rookie season and the farm system -- led by Josuar Gonzalez -- is intriguing, those contracts look like a drag on the franchise's future.

Seattle Mariners: F

On July 5, the Mariners beat Toronto 4-0 for their second straight shutout win and third in four games, thus finishing their first half at 47-44 and in first place in the AL West. It hadn't been a smooth ride, but they looked like the best team in a weak division and FanGraphs agreed, giving them a 63% chance of winning the division and 85% of making the playoffs. If Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodriguez got going, they might even cruise to the division title.

Alas ... disaster, disappointment and despair. The Mariners were plus-27 in run differential through July 5 and are minus-90 since, with only the A's, Rockies and Reds allowing more runs. Raleigh and Rodriguez never really did get going, and the rotation, the supposed strength of the team, ranks in the bottom five of the majors in ERA since that date.

The problems were across the board, however: 28th in runs scored, poor defense (26th in defensive runs saved), and closer Andres Munoz is tied for the MLB lead with 10 blown saves. Dan Wilson is certainly out as manager, and president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto has now made the playoffs just twice in his 11 seasons running the team. If only the Mariners had won 54% of their games.

stories.headline: Arman Tsarukyan elevates his position in MMA divisional rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
Arman Tsarukyan put on a performance at UFC 331 that makes him all but undeniable as the next challenger for the lightweight championship.

Tsarukyan has been in this position before. In January 2025, he pulled out of a title fight because of injury one day before he was to fight for the belt. Later in the year, he was twice passed over when the UFC was booking title bouts. But Saturday's elbow to the face of Mauricio Ruffy gave Tsarukyan the impressive first-round knockout he needed to position himself as the likely first challenger of champion Justin Gaethje.

Tsarukyan's victory also boosted him above former champion Ilia Topuria to No. 2 at lightweight in the latest ESPN divisional rankings.

That is the only movement in the rankings, as Saturday's main event winner, men's flyweight champion Joshua Van, already was the top-ranked 125 pounder. Ex-champ Alexandre Pantoja remains at No. 2.

stories.headline: F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?
stories.summary: The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.
stories.body:
The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.

Most drivers secured short-term deals to survive the regulation shift, leaving the grid wide open for the following year. With only a handful of drivers locked into long-term contracts almost every seat on the grid is up for grabs.

Here is our early look at what the future holds for the current Formula 1 lineup.

McLaren

Lando Norris - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2030

Prior to the start of the 2024 F1 season Norris agreed to an "extended multi-year contract beyond 2025."

The reigning champion has now signed a new contract with McLaren until at least 2030. The deal, which includes one of his title-winning Formula 1 cars as a gift from the team, also has the option of a "multi-year" extension beyond 2030.

Oscar Piastri - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Ahead of the first race of the 2025 F1 season Piastri also signed a multi-year contract extension. His previous deal already ran until the end of 2026, and his latest agreement is likely to keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2028 -- though speculation continues to rumble on about his long-term future.

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton - 2027

While an exact end date of Hamilton's contract -- signed after completing one of the biggest driver moves in F1 history -- was never officially communicated, Hamilton admitted earlier this year that he still had a contract in place for 2027. That means he got at least a three-year deal at Ferrari, something he had also been seeking at Mercedes.

Amid retirement rumours, Hamilton has also crushed speculation and assured fans that he wasn't going anywhere just yet.

He said: "There's a lot of people that are trying to retire me, and that's not even in my thoughts. I'm already thinking of what will be next, and planning for, like, the next five years. But I still plan to be here for some time."

Charles Leclerc - 2028

Leclerc, who first joined Ferrari in 2019, signed another multi-year extension ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

The team did not publicly reveal an exact expiry date, but the new agreement is understood to take Leclerc to 2028 and potentially beyond, giving Ferrari long-term security over one side of its driver lineup.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen - 2030

Red Bull confirmed in 2022 that four-time world champion Verstappen would remain with the team until the end of 2028 in one of the longest deals on the F1 grid.

Sources told ESPN that performance-related clauses in Verstappen's contract could allow him to leave early, but the Dutchman has now signed a new contract extension with Red Bull until 2030 ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Isack Hadjar - 2027

Isack Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to partner Verstappen for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie campaign. He has now signed a contract extension with Red Bull, securing his seat for the 2027 season.

Mercedes

George Russell - beyond 2026

Russell agreed a new deal with Mercedes ahead of the 2026 season following lengthy negotiations with team principal Toto Wolff.

Although the agreement was initially confirmed as taking him through at least 2026, Russell has since described it as a multi-year deal and said he will fulfill the performance clauses in his contract to stay at Mercedes next year.

Kimi Antonelli - TBC

Mercedes' Antonelli has only been given one-year contracts since his debut, but given his form this season there's no way he'll be leaving the Silver Arrows. Right?

No official announcements have been made yet, but Antonelli could be celebrating both a maiden title and a bumper new deal this year.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso - TBC

Alonso's current Aston Martin deal runs until the end of the 2026 season, and he said a decision on his future will come later in the year. At 45 years old, the decision is likely to be between continuing with an underperforming Aston Martin team, or calling time on his F1 career once and for all.

Lance Stroll - TBC

Stroll signed a contract extension in 2024 which kept him with Aston Martin for 2025 "and beyond," but no specific end date was announced. Part of that ambiguity, of course, is because he's the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll.

He remains with the team for 2026, although his position for 2027 has not formally been confirmed.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly - 2028

Gasly is one of the drivers whose future is already settled -- the Frenchman signed a new multi-year agreement with Alpine in 2025 which keeps him locked in at the team until at least the end of the 2028 season.

Franco Colapinto - 2027

Colapinto retained his Alpine seat alongside Gasly for 2026 after taking over from Jack Doohan during the previous season. He has now signed a new contract with the team, meaning the Argentinian will continue with Alpine for the 2027 season.

Haas

Esteban Ocon - TBC

Ocon joined Haas ahead of the 2025 season on a multi-year agreement after leaving Alpine which will run through to the end of the 2026 season. It is unclear whether his current deal guarantees him a place on the 2027 grid.

Oliver Bearman - TBC

Bearman also joined Haas on a multi-year deal when he became a full-time F1 driver in 2025. Like Ocon, the exact duration of Bearman's contract has not been made public, leaving his 2027 status uncertain for now.

However, sources with good knowledge of the team's thinking have told ESPN that Bearman is almost certain to stay with the team in 2027 unless a Ferrari seat opens up, then the Englishman remains effectively loaned to Haas.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson - TBC

Lawson remained with Racing Bulls for 2026 after rebuilding his season following a short-lived promotion to Red Bull the previous year.

His seat is only confirmed for the current season, meaning the New Zealander will again have to prove his case if he is to stay within the Red Bull set-up in 2027.

Arvid Lindblad - TBC

Lindblad became the latest Red Bull junior to make the jump to Formula 1 when he was handed a Racing Bulls seat for 2026.

The rookie is currently only confirmed for this season and the team have played down speculation over their driver lineup for 2027. You'd be shocked to see him go anywhere, though.

Williams

Carlos Sainz - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Sainz originally joined Williams on a deal covering the 2025 and 2026 seasons, with "options to extend" his stay beyond that. He has recently spoken about wanting to make the Williams project work, leading to him signing a new multi-year extension with the team.

Alex Albon - 2027

Albon signed a new one-year contract with Williams during the summer break, tying him down for the 2027 season. The short-term deal is interesting, given Albon's last contract -- signed in 2024 -- was for multiple years. Keeping those options open?

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg - TBC

Hulkenberg joined Sauber ahead of its transformation into the Audi team on a multi-year contract in 2025.

There are believed to be options in his deal which could allow him to remain with Audi beyond 2026, but an exact end date has not been announced.

Gabriel Bortoleto - TBC

Bortoleto joined Hulkenberg at Sauber before the team's transition to Audi and also signed a multi-year deal.

The Brazilian is contracted through at least the end of 2026, but his place for 2027 has not yet been officially confirmed.

Cadillac

Sergio Perez - 2027

Perez returned to the Formula 1 grid with Cadillac for the team's debut season in 2026 after spending a year away from racing.

The Mexican joined on a multi-year agreement understood to be on similar terms to teammate Valtteri Bottas, putting him in line to remain with Cadillac for 2027.

Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Bottas also returned to a full-time race seat with Cadillac after spending 2025 as Mercedes' reserve driver.

The Finn signed a multi-year deal which runs until at least the end of 2027, giving the new team one of the few already settled driver pairings heading into next season.

stories.headline: Stanley Cup contender tiers: Where do all 32 NHL teams fit in?
stories.summary: We slotted all 32 NHL teams into one of six groups heading into the 2026-27 season.
stories.body:
The seasons are changing and the days are getting shorter. That means hockey season is nearly upon us -- and we should be in for a fascinating one in 2026-27.

Going into last season, we wrote that something had to give: Either we would see more of the same after two consecutive Florida Panthers-Edmonton Oilers Stanley Cup Finals, or someone new was finally going to get a chance to break through. Little did we know just how far things would swing away from the familiar.

Not only did the two-time defending Cup winner (and three-time defending East champ) Panthers not win again, but they didn't even make the playoffs amid an injury-wrecked campaign. Meanwhile, the Oilers barely made it any further, losing in the first round to the upstart Anaheim Ducks.

But if we thought the Carolina Hurricanes' long-awaited title after seven previously fruitless playoff trips signals the start of a new NHL era, well, not so fast. The Panthers and Oilers are still here, along with the 2023 champion Vegas Golden Knights -- whom Carolina beat for the Cup -- plus the Colorado Avalanche and Tampa Bay Lightning among recent champs.

If anything, the league now enters another new season with an unusual mix of teams trying to prove last year was no fluke, familiar heavyweights trying to climb back to the top, and young squads trying to crash the party ahead of schedule.

To help handicap the race before opening night on Tuesday, let's look at my aggregated market-forecast tracker, which normalizes and averages together the odds from multiple different sportsbooks and prediction markets to produce a consensus estimate of each team's chances at the playoffs and the Stanley Cup. Using those numbers, we can sort all 32 teams into six tiers -- from the leading Cup favorites to the longest of long shots.

How to watch the 2026-27 NHL season on ESPN networks -- including 100 exclusive games and the out-of-market package (over 1,050 games).

Tier 1: The cream of the crop

Florida Panthers
10.5% Cup | 81.6% playoffs

Last season's injury-riddled disaster apparently did little to shake the market's faith in the Panthers' dynasty. Instead, Florida is right back where it spent most of the previous few years, atop the list of Stanley Cup favorites, as if nothing happened.

And there are reasons to think the Panthers can do a classic "gap year" turnaround -- ranging from the offseason acquisition of Brady Tkachuk (uniting with brother Matthew) to the return of Aleksander Barkov from the knee injury that cost him all of 2025-26, among many, many injured Cats from a year ago.

But as much talent as they have, the Panthers need to prove they can stay healthy and snap back to their previous form, which can't be completely assumed. There's a reason that teams such as the NBA's 2022 Warriors are so rare -- usually when the window is shut, it stays that way.

The biggest uncertainty of all might be in net, where Jacob Markstrom and Akira Schmid replace Sergei Bobrovsky -- particularly after Florida already ranked 28th in goalie GAR with Bobrovsky last year.

Big question: Was 2025-26 merely a mulligan?

Colorado Avalanche
9.8% Cup | 89.9% playoffs

The Avs belong here until proven otherwise, after dominating the regular season essentially wire-to-wire. (Never mind how things ended in the playoffs, when they set new NHL records for being swept by a Vegas team with 16 fewer wins and a goal differential 84 goals worse during the season.)

As long as this core of Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar and Martin Necas & Co. are together -- which got further solidified when Makar signed an eight-year, $163 million contract extension last month -- Colorado has as good a Cup shot as anyone. But out of its nine straight playoff trips, it has made just one Cup Final (winning the 2022 title) and one other Western Conference final. Oh, and this was also one of the oldest teams in hockey last season.

Big question: How many more great seasons can the Avalanche afford to waste?

Carolina Hurricanes
9.6% Cup | 85.1% playoffs

Carolina, maybe the model NHL franchise for stability, could have fewer question marks than the others in this tier, which is good news for its hopes of running things back after winning the Cup a year ago.

Under coach Rod Brind'Amour and an exceptionally deep corps of talent led by Sebastian Aho, the Canes finally prevailed through the power of persistence and belief in their possession-heavy system.

Now they bring back most of the same group, save for officially moving on from Frederik Andersen at goalie in favor of Cup Final breakout Brandon Bussi and Pyotr Kochetkov. They may even improve by leaning more on young Logan Stankoven and Jackson Blake, who stepped their games up in the playoffs.

Big question: Does the dam break open from here?

Tier 2: Still heavyweights

Edmonton Oilers
7.8% Cup | 85.5% playoffs

No longer are the Oilers automatically penciled into the very highest tier of contenders, which is the cost of a season where Edmonton wasn't quite as sharp -- especially on the goal-prevention side -- and didn't have as much depth outside of Connor McDavid, Leon Draisaitl and Evan Bouchard. This echoes the classic problem of the McDavid era before they started to make deeper playoff runs.

But they also made a lot of wholesale changes, from a new coach (Mike Babcock) to a reworked goaltending mix (both Connor Ingram and Stuart Skinner are gone) and a new blue-line mainstay with Darnell Nurse leaving for San Jose.

Any team with their top-line talent is dangerous, but the clock is also ticking with McDavid signed for just two more seasons.

Big question: Will the goaltending be any better with Frederik Andersen, Tristan Jarry and Devon Levi?

Vegas Golden Knights
6.8% Cup | 83.2% playoffs

The Golden Knights are one of the toughest teams to fit in any tier because it's impossible to know exactly what to expect from them this season.

During the 2025-26 regular season -- almost entirely spent under former coach Bruce Cassidy -- Vegas had a middle-of-the-road +0.18 goals per game differential and lost more games (43) than it won (39) ... leading to a late-season switch to John Tortorella, which worked wonders as the Knights won 14 of their first 19 playoff games ... before dropping three straight to lose in the Cup Final.

Now Vegas is hoping that improved health -- only Florida lost more cap-hit dollars to injuries -- and the leadership of new coach Ryan Craig (previously an assistant with the team) will lead to a more normal contending campaign.

Big question: How many times can a team keep reinventing itself -- and keep winning?

Tier 3: The next wave

Tampa Bay Lightning
5.8% Cup | 75.6% playoffs

Speaking of confusing teams, the Bolts land here after somehow following three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances (including two wins) with four straight first-round playoff losses.

The good news is that Tampa Bay proved its dynasty can resist decline, continuing to thrive in the regular season with a +0.82 goals-per-game differential over the past two seasons (second best behind Colorado's +0.87). But as great as Nikita Kucherov and Andrei Vasilevskiy are, this core isn't getting any younger -- and it lost one of its best producers from 2025-26, Darren Raddysh, in a summer sign-and-trade.

Big question: Did Tampa Bay just forget how to make deep postseason runs?

Minnesota Wild
5.5% Cup | 81.0% playoffs

Long stuck in the NHL's good-but-not-great tier, the Wild are legitimately higher than that now. That happened thanks to a highly talented core of skaters -- including Kirill Kaprizov, Matt Boldy, Brock Faber and, after a midseason trade, Quinn Hughes -- plus Jesper Wallstedt in net.

They even managed to win their first playoff series since 2015, upsetting their spiritual rival Dallas Stars (i.e., the former Minnesota North Stars).

But the following series, a 4-1 defeat to Colorado, showed how much more the Wild have to improve if they want to keep leveling up.

Big question: Can they find a way to improve at center? (No Wild pivot had 10+ GAR a year ago.)

Washington Capitals
5.1% Cup | 69.1% playoffs

Washington's biggest star is 41-year-old Alex Ovechkin, and the team is desperate for one last run with him despite missing the playoffs a year ago.

Framed that way, the 2026-27 Caps sound like an all-time great's sad swan song.

But actually, there are a lot of reasons for excitement in the nation's capital. For one thing, the Caps were better than your typical non-playoff team; they had a better regulation points percentage than multiple East playoff squads last season. stories.headline: Mikel Arteta agrees a new long-term contract extension with Arsenal - sources
stories.summary: Arsenal are expected to announce Mikel Arteta has signed a new long-term contract after the 44-year-old agreed terms to stay on as manager, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
Arsenal are expected to announce Mikel Arteta has signed a new long-term contract after the 44-year-old agreed terms to stay on as manager, sources have told ESPN.

Arteta's current deal expires at the end of the season but the Spaniard has repeatedly stated his intention to remain at the club he joined in December 2019.

Sources say all parties have been relaxed about the situation for several months with an agreement likely to be finalised during a pause in the domestic campaign.

Arsenal do not play again until Oct 10 as a result of the newly-extended international break and confirmation that Arteta has signed a new contract could come before then.

The Gunners declined to comment when contacted by ESPN but Arteta is set for a significant pay rise on his current salary which sources say can reach £15m ($20m) with bonuses.

- Mourinho's ref rants overshadow Madrid derby defeat; can Arsenal shrug off heavy loss?

"I'm extremely happy and I feel very grateful to work with the people I work with," said Arteta when asked about his contract situation last week.

Arteta ended Arsenal's 22-year wait for a Premier League title in May and last month, he registered his 150th league win from 249 games -- only Pep Guardiola, Jose Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Sir Alex Ferguson have achieved the milestone quicker.

stories.headline: Lions make call on Neale Grand Final ban appeal
stories.summary: Brisbane will head to the AFL appeals board in a desperate bid to free suspended star Lachie Neale for the grand final.
stories.body:
Lachie Neale has faced a monster media pack on arrival in Melbourne as the star Brisbane midfielder appeals his suspension for the AFL grand final.

Neale remains banned for Saturday's premiership decider against Fremantle after failing to argue his way out of a one-match suspension for a gut punch on Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan.

The dual Brownlow medallist gave a short statement after arriving at Melbourne Airport with Lions teammates on Wednesday.

"Very hopeful that it's successful, but regardless of the result, I'll be here to support the boys and the club," Neale said.

"It's a big week for the club."

Following the 15-second statement, Neale was chased by cameras as he immediately left the Virgin Australia terminal.

Fellow Lions veteran Dayne Zorko conducted a press conference after Neale's departure, with the majority of questions focused on the dual premiership co-captain.

Neale was also the story of grand final week last year, famously overcoming a calf injury to play a second-half cameo in Brisbane's demolition of Geelong.

"Lots of scrutiny last year about whether he'd play, whether he wouldn't," Zorko said.

"(20)24 he had a broken foot, so we're used to it.

"It's a lot (the attention), but he seems to be fine.

"I sat next to him on the plane.

"He's just taking it in his stride."

To succeed at an appeals board hearing on Thursday at 4pm, Brisbane will have to prove the tribunal finding was either an error of law, an unreasonable decision, a manifestly excessive classification, or a manifestly excessive sanction.

"There's been 10 (gut punch) incidents this year, all of them have resulted in a week (suspension)," the AFL's footy boss Greg Swann told reporters on Wednesday.

"That was the third (tribunal) appeal and they've all been upheld."

At the end of a four-and-a-half hour hearing on Tuesday night, the tribunal decided not to enact the 'exceptional and compelling clause' to allow Neale to avoid suspension.

Why? For many reasons, according to tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC.

There was Neale's evidence, which Gleeson rejected as "inconsistent".

Neale insisted he didn't strike Ginnivan during last Saturday night's preliminary final.

"We have listened carefully to Mr Neale's evidence but we find it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video," Gleeson said.

Neale maintained his shoulder and chest made contact with Ginnivan; the tribunal found it was "a forceful blow delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand".

That's the guilty part. Next was what Gleeson described as "the more difficult issue".

Was using the exceptional and compelling circumstances clause justified to downgrade Neale's penalty from a ban to a fine?

Introduced this year, the clause had been deployed once: to downgrade a one-game ban to Collingwood legend and the AFL's games record holder Scott Pendlebury, to a fine.

But Gleeson noted Pendlebury was charged with rough conduct. Specifically, graded as careless conduct, medium impact, and high contact.

Neale was charged with striking graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

Then, there was Neale's record, which his barrister - the AFL's former football operations boss, Adrian Anderson - compared to Pendlebury.

Until Tuesday night, Neale had never been banned in a 15-year career including two Brownlow medals, six club champion awards, and captaining the Lions to two premierships.
